strengths: Simple, elegant, and well-motivated approach that models task progress as a frame-wise temporal distance prediction problem, supported by a neat theoretical connection to potential-based reward shaping.

Excellent empirical results across 10 Meta-World tasks, showing superior performance and sample efficiency compared to strong baselines like VIP, Rank2Reward, and PROGRESSOR, and even outperforming the default hand-engineered environment rewards.
Convincing cross-domain transfer experiments utilizing real-world human demonstration videos, demonstrating the robustness of the learned representations and scalability to out-of-domain data.

Extremely thorough ablation studies validating each designed component of the method (implicit negative sampling, exponentially weighted sampling, discretization) as well as comparing against alternative temporal modeling architectures.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on the sparse environment success signal: According to Appendix A.3.2 (Figure 12), when the sparse environment success reward is completely removed, the policy success rate drops to zero across all tasks within the 200,000-step budget. This crucial limitation of relying on the sparse reward should be discussed more prominently in the main text.

Assumption of linear temporal progress: The framework relies on the assumption that task progress is linearly correlated with time steps. For tasks with highly non-uniform dynamics (e.g., long pauses followed by rapid changes), temporal distance might not reflect actual physical progress accurately. The manuscript would benefit from a discussion on how variable-speed demonstrations affect the model.

strengths: Simple yet highly effective conceptual formulation: Modeling dense robotic rewards as the temporal distance between frame pairs is intuitive and successfully leverages the natural progression of expert demonstrations.

Well-designed components: The paper introduces key technical ingredients—namely, implicit negative sampling (for suboptimality awareness), exponentially weighted pair sampling (for fine-grained temporal resolution), and two-hot discretization—which are thoroughly ablated and proven critical for stability and performance.

Impressive empirical performance: TimeRewarder consistently outperforms both state-of-the-art representation-based reward methods (e.g., VIP, PROGRESSOR) and, notably, the hand-crafted Meta-World environment rewards in terms of sample efficiency and final success rate.
Cross-domain transfer: The experiments demonstrating reward learning from passive human videos to guide a virtual robot show great promise for scaling RL using in-the-wild video data.
Comprehensive evaluation and clarity: The paper is exceptionally well-written, with high-quality visualizations of the progress curves (Figure 4) and extensive baselines.
weaknesses: Dependence on sparse success signals: In the absence of the sparse environmental success reward (as shown in Figure 12 / Appendix A.3.2), the model fails to achieve success within 200k frames. This suggests that the learned temporal distance reward acts primarily as an exploratory shaper and still heavily relies on the binary success indicator to complete the task.
Sensitivity to hyperparameters: Analysis regarding the sensitivity of the hyperparameters, specifically the sampling parameter $\lambda$ and the discretization bin size $K$, is lacking.

Limitation under non-monotonic or cyclic tasks: The temporal distance model assumes that progress is strictly monotonic with respect to time. For complex manipulation tasks requiring back-and-forth movements, re-try loops, or multi-stage sub-tasks with arbitrary order, this formulation might provide misleading or contradictory reward signals.

strengths: The core idea of using frame-wise temporal distance from passive videos as a dense progress-based reward signal is intuitive and well-motivated.
The evaluation is quite extensive, covering 10 Meta-World tasks and comparing against many competitive baselines (VIP, Rank2Reward, PROGRESSOR, GAIfO, ADS, etc.).
The cross-domain experiments using real-world human videos to assist robot learning is a great addition, demonstrating the practical potential of the method.
The paper provides a detailed ablation study of the individual components (discretization, negative sampling, weighted sampling) as well as alternative modeling choices.
weaknesses: Theoretical issues with reward shaping: The learned reward is defined directly as the network's prediction $r_{\text{TR}}(o_t, o_{t+1}) = F_\theta(o_t, o_{t+1})$. Because it does not decompose into a potential difference $V(o_{t+1}) - V(o_t)$, it is not potential-based. This makes the RL process theoretically vulnerable to reward hacking, where the agent can exploit approximation errors in $F_\theta$ to accumulate positive rewards through cyclic behaviors (loops).

Dependency on the sparse success reward: As demonstrated in Appendix A.3.2 (Figure 12), when the sparse environment reward is completely removed, TimeRewarder achieves a 0% success rate across all 10 tasks. This indicates that the learned proxy reward is not self-sufficient and heavily relies on an external sparse success detector. This critical limitation is largely omitted from the main text, which somewhat overstates the ability of the method to enable reward-free RL.

Incomplete and potentially misleading baseline curves: In Figure 5, the 'Environment reward' (which uses the ground-truth dense reward) is plotted as a flat dashed line. Since this is an online RL baseline trained on the same environment, it should have an active learning curve over the 200k frames. Representing it as a flat line hides its training progress and makes the comparison less transparent.

Incremental novelty: The methodological components (two-hot discretization, exponential pair sampling, predicting temporal distance) are mostly adapted from existing literature. While their combination works well, the technical contribution over related works like PROGRESSOR or Rank2Reward is relatively incremental.

strengths: Simple yet highly effective formulation: Modeling temporal distance between frame pairs using a classification objective with two-hot discretization is elegant and robust.

Comprehensive and strong empirical results: Outperforms a wide variety of state-of-the-art baselines on 10 Meta-World tasks and even surpasses manually designed environment dense rewards on most tasks.

Thorough ablation studies and analysis: The paper meticulously ablates its key components (implicit negative sampling, weighted sampling, and two-hot discretization) and provides insightful visualizations (PCA, reward curves, and VOC metric).

Real-world cross-domain generalization: Successfully demonstrates that the method can utilize cross-domain, unlabeled human video demonstrations to boost RL performance when in-domain robot demonstrations are extremely scarce.
weaknesses: Reliance on sparse success signal: While sparse success is much easier to obtain than dense rewards, the downstream RL performance heavily relies on the joint reward (proxy dense + sparse success). As shown in Appendix A.4.5, training with only the proxy reward without a sparse success signal yields significantly lower success rates within the 200k steps budget.

Handling of visual aliasing and cyclic behaviors: Although the paper theoretically discusses visual aliasing in POMDPs (Section 4.3) and proposes utilizing frame histories as a solution, it is not fully explored or systematically benchmarked on tasks with high-frequency back-and-forth motions in the main experimental section.

strengths: Simple, elegant, and intuitive formulation: modeling dense task progress as a frame-wise temporal distance prediction problem with self-supervised learning from passive videos.
Extensive experiments across 10 challenging Meta-World tasks and the ManiSkill3 PushCube task, showing significant performance gains and high sample efficiency.
Outperforms existing state-of-the-art visual reward learning methods (e.g., VIP, Rank2Reward, PROGRESSOR) and even hand-crafted environment dense rewards on most tasks.

Thorough analysis, including value-order correlation, PCA visualization of representation spaces, and detailed ablation studies of each component (implicit negative sampling, weighted sampling, and discretization).
Cross-domain validation using real-world human videos, demonstrating the method's potential for scaling using diverse, unlabeled video sources.
weaknesses: Reliance on sparse success signals: As shown in Appendix A.4.5, without the sparse success reward, the agent fails to achieve success within 200,000 steps. The method's effectiveness is partially reliant on the availability of this success signal, which should be discussed more prominently in the main text.

Sensitivity to non-monotonic or cyclic tasks: The paper notes that back-and-forth motions can violate the monotonic assumption. Although history-conditioned models are suggested as a theoretical fix, this is not systematically evaluated in the experiments.

Evaluation is limited to simulation: Although real-world human video datasets are used for cross-domain reward learning, the RL policy training and execution are kept entirely in simulation (Meta-World and ManiSkill3). Real-world robot execution would make the validation stronger.

strengths: Simple, elegant, and effective formulation: Modeling dense rewards through frame-wise signed temporal distances is highly intuitive and naturally incorporates implicit negative sampling to penalize regressive behavior.

Well-motivated design choices: The use of Weighted Pair Sampling (to emphasize step-wise adjacent frame relationships) and Two-hot Discretization (for numerical stability and capturing sharp transitions) are mathematically justified and thoroughly ablated.

Extensive empirical evaluation: Evaluated across 10 Meta-World manipulation tasks, demonstrating outstanding sample efficiency and success rates. It consistently outperforms 8 competitive baselines, as well as the hand-designed environmental dense rewards in 9 out of 10 tasks.

Strong analysis and visualizations: The paper provides great qualitative and quantitative depth, including Value-Order Correlation (VOC) metrics, PCA visualizations of the learned representation space, and detailed reward curves for successful versus failed rollouts.

Cross-domain transfer: Demonstrates practical utility by successfully incorporating real-world, unlabeled human videos to improve downstream robot learning in simulation, even with highly limited in-domain data.
weaknesses: Continued reliance on sparse success signals: Although common in reward-learning literature, the primary RL experiments still rely on a combined sparse success signal. Performance drops significantly when relying solely on the learned proxy reward (as shown in Appendix A.4.5).

Handling of visual aliasing: While the authors theoretically discuss utilizing observation histories to address visual aliasing in back-and-forth motions, the main experiments rely on single-frame inputs, leaving the practical efficacy of history-based extension largely un-evaluated.

Sensitivity to varying demonstration lengths: The temporal distance calculation is normalized by the horizon length (T - 1). It remains unclear how robust the method is when learning from expert trajectories that have highly variable execution speeds or varying sequence lengths.
